title: Heschel at Selma (1965)
hookLine: Abraham Joshua Heschel marches with Martin Luther King and calls it a kind of prayer

cards: Arms linked, a long column of marchers sets out along the highway from Selma, Alabama, for Montgomery, to demand the right to vote.
In the front row, a few places from Martin Luther King Jr., walks a man with a white beard and a cap, in a coat and tie, a garland of flowers around his neck.
He is Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel, a scholar who spent his life writing about prayer. When he got home, he said this march had been a kind of prayer too.

teach.h: A RABBI WHO WROTE ABOUT PRAYER.
teach.b: Heschel came from a family of Hasidic rabbis in Poland and got out of Europe before the war. Much of his family did not. In America he taught and wrote about prayer, the Sabbath, and the prophets.
The prophets fascinated him because they couldn't stay quiet when someone was being crushed.
In Selma, Black Americans had been beaten for trying to register to vote, and marchers had already been attacked on a bridge out of town. King called on clergy to come. Heschel came.
Afterward, he wrote that he felt as if his legs were praying. For him, prayer wasn't only words read from a book. It could be a whole body moving toward justice.
The prophet Amos talks this way.

teach.h: LET JUSTICE WELL UP AS WATERS.
teach.b: Speaking for God to people who trample the poor, he says their feasts and the noise of their songs are not wanted, and then: "But let justice well up as waters, And righteousness as a mighty stream."
King used that line too, in his own wording, from pulpits and podiums. Two men from two traditions, walking in step, carrying the same prophet.
This doesn't mean marching replaces praying; Heschel kept praying in the synagogue. It means the wall between the two can be thin. A walk can begin with a prayer.

how: Heschel's march at Selma is retold in synagogues and Jewish schools, often around Martin Luther King Jr. Day, as an example of prayer joined to action for justice.

go, and walk near the front.
games.why: Heschel went and walked in the front row with King. afterward he wrote that his legs were praying.

practice: If you can, stand and take a slow walk, across the room or down a hall; if walking isn't possible, let your hands or your breath keep a slow, steady beat.
As you move, bring to mind one cause you care about, or one person who needs justice, and let each step, or each breath, be for them. If you pray, let the walking be your prayer.
